name: <header> <nav> <main> <aside> <footer>
desc: The page level landmarks. Each element gives the browser a role and gives screen reader users a jump target.
example:
Skip to content
Riverside Hotel
Rooms Bookings

Bookings

One upcoming stay.

12 Dock Street, Budapest
body:
Landmarks in the accessibility tree: **header** becomes banner, **nav** becomes navigation, **main** becomes main, **aside** becomes complementary, **footer** becomes contentinfo. The first and last only keep those roles when they are not nested inside article, aside, main, nav or section.

Rules that carry marks:
- One visible main per page, one h1.
- Every nav beyond the first needs its own label.
- A section needs a heading or a label before it becomes a region.
- Landmarks are siblings; do not put main inside header or nav.

name: <header>
desc: Introductory content for the page or for the nearest article. At top level it is the banner landmark; inside an article it is the article masthead.
example:
Riverside Hotel

...

Quiet rooms, slow breakfast

Published 2 March 2026

The room faced the river.
body:
A header inside article, aside, main, nav or section is not the page banner. That scoping rule is why several header elements on one page are normal, and why a header around the top of a sidebar is not a landmark.

Do not use header for a block that merely sits at the top. If it does not introduce the content below it, use a div.

name: <nav>
desc: A major block of navigation links. Each nav on a page needs a distinct label so the landmark list stays usable.
example:
• Rooms
  • Bookings
  1. Home
  2. Bookings
body:
A single link in a paragraph is not navigation. A footer list of social links usually is not either. The main menu, a table of contents, breadcrumbs and pagination are.

Unlabelled duplicates are announced as navigation twice, so the user has to visit both to tell them apart. The newer search element wraps a search form and gives it its own landmark.

name: <main>
desc: The content unique to this page. It must not sit inside header, footer, nav, aside or article, and there is one visible main per page.
example:
Skip to main content

Bookings

Upcoming stays

Check-in on 12 March.
body:
tabindex="-1" makes main programmatically focusable, so the skip link can move focus into it. Without it some browsers scroll but leave focus on the link, and the next Tab press returns to the menu.

Several main elements are allowed only when all but one are hidden. That is a single page app pattern, not a normal page.

name: <section>
desc: A thematic group of content, normally introduced by a heading. It becomes a region landmark only when it has an accessible name.
example:
Upcoming stays

One stay in March.

...
body:
An unnamed section is generic, so it gives nothing that a div would not give. Use section when the block would appear in a table of contents, and div when the block exists for CSS.

Heading level follows structure: h2 for a section inside the page, h3 for a section inside a section.

name: <article>
desc: A self-contained composition that would still make sense on its own, such as a post, a review or a comment. It should have its own heading.
example:
Quiet rooms, slow breakfast

2 March 2026

The room faced the river.

Comments

Reply from the hotel

Breakfast now starts at 6:30.
body: The test is syndication: could this block move to another page or a feed and still stand? If yes, article. A product card in a grid often fails that test and is better as a list item or a div.

name: <aside>
desc: Content related to the main flow but not part of it: a sidebar, a note, related links. It becomes the complementary landmark at top level.
example:
Bookings

The booking details.

Need help?

Reception is open from 7:00 to 22:00.

Call +36 1 234 5678
body:
An aside nested inside an article is a note about that article and does not appear as a top level complementary landmark. That is expected.

Never put the price, the booking form or anything the user must act on inside an aside. If it is required, it belongs in main.

name: <footer>
desc: Closing content for the page or the nearest article: contact details, copyright, related links. Top level it is the contentinfo landmark.
example:
Riverside Hotel
12 Dock Street
front@example.test

Prices include VAT.
body:
A footer inside article, aside, main, nav or section is not contentinfo. An article footer holds tags or the author, which is a valid and common use.

The address element is for contact details of the page or article, not for every postal address in the text.

name: <figure> and <figcaption>
desc: A figure groups content the text refers to, with an optional caption. The caption must be the first or the last child.
example: The room has a balcony facing the river.
body:
The alt text describes the image for someone who cannot see it. The caption is visible text that explains why the image is there. Repeating the same sentence in both makes a screen reader say it twice.

A figure is not required for every image. Use it when the text points at the image or the caption adds information. A decorative image uses alt="" and needs no figure.

name: <details> and <summary>
desc: A native disclosure widget. Summary is the always visible label and the click target; the rest is shown when the element is open.
example:
Questions

Can I change the dates?

Yes, up to 48 hours before check-in, from the booking page.

Is breakfast included?

Yes, from 6:30 to 10:00.
body:
Summary must be the first child of details. The browser handles focus and the Enter and Space keys, and it announces expanded or collapsed. No JavaScript is needed, and nothing breaks when scripts fail.

Closed content is removed from the accessibility tree, so do not hide essential text there. The name attribute on several details elements builds an exclusive accordion, where opening one closes the others. Do not build a navigation menu out of details; it is announced as a disclosure, not a menu.

name: aria-label and aria-labelledby
desc: Gives a landmark or a section its accessible name. aria-labelledby points at visible text; aria-label supplies text that is not on screen.
example:
...
...

Upcoming stays

...
body:
aria-label is a string. aria-labelledby takes one or more ids and uses their text content. If visible text already names the block, aria-labelledby is usually the better choice.

Do not label every nav "Navigation". Repeated names tell the user nothing. Do not add aria-label to an element that already has a visible heading unless the heading is not descriptive.

name: <caption>
desc: Names the table. It must be the first child of table, and screen readers announce it when the table is entered.
example:
Room prices in EUR, one night, March 2026
Room Price
Double 80
body:
A heading above the table is not part of the table and is not announced as its name. The caption is.

State unit and period when they are not obvious: prices in EUR, per night, including breakfast. A caption on a layout table is a sign that the table should not exist.

name: <thead> <tbody> <tfoot>
desc: Row groups. Thead holds header rows, tbody the data, tfoot the summary. Browsers insert tbody around any bare tr.
example:
Bookings, March 2026
Guest Nights
Booking 1041 2
Total 2
body:
The parser inserts tbody, so a CSS selector of table > tr matches nothing in the live DOM. Write tbody tr or table > tbody > tr.

Several tbody elements can group rows, for example one per city. Thead repeats on each printed page in most browsers, which is one reason to use the element rather than styling the first row.

name: colspan
desc: Makes a cell cover several columns. The row still has to account for the same total number of column slots as every other row.
example:
Price per night in EUR, by season
Room Price per night
Spring Summer Winter
Double 80 110 70
Average double room price: 87
body:
Count slots, not cells. A cell with colspan 3 takes three slots in its row. The widest row decides the column count, and a row that adds one slot too many silently creates an extra column for the whole table.

scope="colgroup" on the spanning header tells assistive technology that the header covers the columns below it. Colspan 0 means "to the end of the group" in the specification and is best avoided.

name: rowspan
desc: Makes a cell cover several rows. The following rows lose one slot each while the span is active.
example:
One night, one room of each type, prices in EUR
Hotel Room Price
Riverside Double 80
Twin 75
Dock View Single 60
body:
A rowspan that reaches past the last row pushes cells into a column that does not exist. Count the slots per row before writing the markup.

Use scope="rowgroup" when the spanning header labels a group of rows. scope="row" is for a header that labels one row only.

name: scope
desc: Tells assistive technology which cells a header covers. Values are col, row, colgroup and rowgroup.
example:
Bookings for March 2026
Guest Room Nights
Booking 1041 Double 2
body:
Without scope the browser assumes auto and guesses from position. The guess fails as soon as a colspan or rowspan appears.

scope is enough for nearly every table in the exam. The headers and id attributes are for irregular tables where a cell has more than one header that scope cannot express.

name: <colgroup> and <col>
desc: Groups columns for width and background styling. Col elements are empty and their count should match the real column count.
example:
Bookings report
Hotel City Check-in Check-out
Riverside Budapest 12 Mar 14 Mar
body:
CSS on col supports only a small set of properties: width, background, border and visibility. Text colour and padding on col do nothing.

span on col covers several columns with one element. If the colgroup declares more columns than the table has, browsers pad or ignore the rest and the widths stop lining up.

name: headers and id
desc: Explicit header association for irregular tables where scope cannot express which headers apply to a cell.
example:
Price by room and season, in EUR
Room Spring Autumn
Double 80 95
body:
The headers attribute takes a space separated list of ids. Order does not matter to assistive technology, but column header before row header is the usual reading order.

Long id lists are hard to maintain, and mixing scope with headers carelessly can make a cell announce the same header twice. Reach for this only after scope stops being enough.

name: <video>
desc: Embeds a video player with native controls. Width and height reserve the box, poster shows a still before playback.
body:
Controls are not optional for content the user is meant to watch. Without them the element is a still frame.

playsinline stops iOS from taking the video fullscreen on its own. autoplay only works when the video is muted in Chrome and Safari, and moving content over five seconds still needs a pause control. The paragraph inside the element is the fallback for browsers without video support and is worth writing every time.

name: <audio>
desc: Embeds an audio player. It has no visual area, so width, height and poster do not apply.
body:
Audio needs a text path. A transcript on the page, or a link to one, is the only way a deaf user gets the content.

The player is small and unlabelled by itself, so the surrounding heading or figure caption must say what it contains.

name: <source>
desc: Offers the browser one file to choose from. The browser takes the first source it can play, using type to skip formats it does not support.
body:
Without type the browser may download the whole file just to discover it cannot play it. With type it can skip the file immediately.

The source list is a preference order, not an error recovery chain. If the chosen file 404s, the browser does not move to the next one. The media attribute on source is for picture, not for video or audio.

name: <track>
desc: Adds timed text to video or audio from a WebVTT file. Kind decides whether it is captions, subtitles, chapters or metadata.
body:
Kinds: subtitles translate dialogue for viewers who can hear it; captions also carry non-speech sounds and are what most pages need; descriptions give text descriptions of the visuals; chapters build a chapter menu; metadata is for scripts.

A WebVTT file starts with WEBVTT, then cues with a timing line such as 00:00:01.000 --> 00:00:04.000 and text lines. Serve it as text/vtt. Cross origin tracks fail silently unless the media element has crossorigin="anonymous" and the track server sends CORS headers.

name: <iframe>
syntax: <iframe src="/embed/map.html" title="Map showing the hotel" width="640" height="360"></iframe>
desc: Embeds another HTML document in its own browsing context. The title is what a screen reader announces for the frame.
example: If the map does not load, open it in a new page.
body:
The frame is a separate document: its own lang, headings, landmarks and focus order. Nothing from the parent page reaches inside, and the embedded page has to be accessible on its own.

Use frames for maps, players, payment forms and document previews, not for the site navigation or the whole page. Always give a direct link to the content as an alternative. Reserve width and height, or the page shifts when the frame loads.

name: sandbox
desc: Restricts what an embedded document may do. An empty value blocks scripts, forms, popups and same-origin access.
example:
<!-- Untrusted third party widget: scripts only, no same-origin access. -->
<iframe
  src="/embed/widget.html"
  title="Availability calendar"
  width="480"
  height="360"
  loading="lazy"
  sandbox="allow-scripts allow-forms">
</iframe>

<!-- Our own map page: scripts and same origin are fine here. -->
<iframe
  src="/embed/map.html"
  title="Map showing Riverside Hotel on Dock Street"
  width="640"
  height="360"
  sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-popups">
</iframe>
body:
Tokens: allow-scripts, allow-same-origin, allow-forms, allow-popups, allow-downloads, allow-presentation, allow-top-navigation-by-user-activation. Start with an empty sandbox and add only what the frame needs.

allow-scripts plus allow-same-origin on a same-origin frame lets the document remove its own sandbox, which defeats the point. Never combine them for content you do not control. Refusing to be framed is a response header (Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors or X-Frame-Options), not an HTML attribute.
